title: Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two
note: Model: synchronous rounds, latency overhead l (rounds from send to delivery), bandwidth overhead beta (noise messages per user per round), N users, K nodes, c compromised, global passive adversary. Thm 2 (synchronised users, l<N, beta*N>=1): no protocol achieves strong anonymity if 2*l*beta < 1 - eps(eta), eps(eta)=1/eta^d, d>0. Thm 4 (K in poly(eta), K>c>=l, l<N): impossible if 2*l*beta < 1-eps or l in O(1) (constant latency excluded once nodes are compromised). Thm 5 (c<l): impossible if 2*(l-c)*beta < 1-eps. Thm 7 (unsynchronised users, each sends with prob p=beta+p0): impossible if 2*l*p < 1-eps. Also delta-sender-anonymity lower bound delta >= 1 - f_beta(l), f_beta(x)=min(1,(x+beta*N*x)/(N-1)) (Thm 1). Ideal asymptotics: l=O(1), beta=O(1/N). Same bounds for recipient anonymity (App. C).
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage sits at the high-bandwidth, low-latency corner of this trade-off: every object is flooded to every node, so recipient ambiguity costs O(N) bandwidth per message and gives no sender protection against a network-level observer.

title: Comprehensive Anonymity Trilemma: User Coordination is not enough
note: Extends the trilemma to protocols with 'user coordination' (DC-net style shares: h+1 users each send a share, receiver cannot tell which is the real sender). With l^ = latency, B = bandwidth overhead (noise per real message), N users, K nodes, c compromised, eps=1/eta^d. Thm 2 (synchronised): no strong anonymity if l^(B+1) < N - eps, or if c >= (B+1)*l^ and l^ in O(1). Thm 5 (unsynchronised, l^<N, B<(N-1)-eps): impossible if p*l^ < 1-eps, and impossible if l^ in O(1). Thm 6: if a constant fraction c/K is compromised and B<(N-1)-eps, impossible when c > l^2 and l^2 in O(log eta). Thm 7: impossible if p*max{l^-c/2, l^} < 1-eps. Thm 3/8 (Anytrust, K-c=gamma in O(1)): impossible unless l^2 > K-gamma (each packet traverses ~sqrt of compromised parties) or massive overhead. Unified condition: l^(p0+beta) < 1-eps. Strong anonymity with coordination needs B >= N-1 (every other user sends a share for every real message).
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage sits at the high-bandwidth, low-latency corner of this trade-off: every object is flooded to every node, so recipient ambiguity costs O(N) bandwidth per message and gives no sender protection against a network-level observer. Coordination (DC-net) escapes the first trilemma only by paying the B>=N-1 bandwidth that flooding already pays.

title: Anonymity Trilemma: Beyond Mix-Nets
venue: Purdue technical report; earlier version of the PoPETs 2020 comprehensive trilemma
note: Earlier full version of the comprehensive trilemma: defines a wider class of AC protocols with out-of-band user coordination (mixnet tricks plus DC-net-style shares), proves that even this class cannot achieve strong anonymity, low latency and low bandwidth together, and derives impossibility conditions (relaxed compared with mixnets). States that the only escape from the trilemma is to leave this class, via 'expensive crypto-magic' such as fully homomorphic onion encryption or efficient amortised secret sharing. Exact conditions as in 2020-das-comprehensivetrilemma.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage sits at the high-bandwidth, low-latency corner of this trade-off: every object is flooded to every node, so recipient ambiguity costs O(N) bandwidth per message and gives no sender protection against a network-level observer.

title: SoK on Performance Bounds in Anonymous Communication
note: Systematises four proven overhead bounds under one privacy-notion hierarchy: (1) Dropping-Bound (Ando-Lysyanskaya-Upfal, 'On the complexity of anonymous communication through public networks'; active drop attack, goal (SR)-bar pair-sender-receiver unlinkability, onion routing/mixnets only); (2) Trilemma (Das et al.; goal (SM)-bar pair-sender-message unlinkability; trade-off bandwidth/latency); (3) Counting-Bound (Gelernter-Herzberg; goal SO-bar, corrupt receivers): 'the protocol cannot deliver more real messages to corrupt receivers than any sender sends in real and dummy messages'; (4) Optimality-Bound (Hevia-Micciancio) shown equivalent to the Counting-Bound. All bounds break only weaker goals than claimed; the paper tightens them (errata: Dropping-Bound needs a corrupted receiver).
bitmessage_link: Shows which privacy goals the bounds actually cover; relevant to what flooding with ciphertext ambiguity can claim against a corrupt receiver.

title: Studying the anonymity trilemma with a discrete-event mix network simulator
note: Open-source discrete-event simulator measuring anonymity, latency and bandwidth overhead jointly; empirical analysis of Elixxir, HOPR and Nym design choices (topology, mixing, cover traffic). No new bound; empirical positions on the trilemma.
bitmessage_link: Provides measured points on the trilemma surface for deployed mixnets, against which flooding costs can be compared.

title: On the Limits of Provable Anonymity
note: Computational anonymity definitions (Comp-N-anonymity: eavesdroppers, malicious peers, malicious destinations). 'Ultimate anonymity' is feasible (Thm 10, via MPC/TTP, polynomial but absurd cost) and the overhead is unavoidable. Thm 13 (deterministic protocols, Comp-SA-anonymous against global eavesdropper destination): for every run and every R, messages reaching the destination Out <= min over honest potential senders p_i of L_i(R) (messages sent by p_i), and total sends Com >= Out * |honest potential senders|. Thm 15 holds the same, up to a negligible term, for probabilistic protocols. In words: delivered real traffic cannot exceed what the least active honest sender emits, so cover traffic must be quadratic in the number of senders.
bitmessage_link: Counting argument: honest senders must each emit as many packets as the total delivered, which flooding (everyone relays everything) satisfies at O(N) cost.

title: Practical and Provably Secure Onion Routing
note: First onion routing protocols provably anonymous (differential-privacy style) against network, passive and active adversaries with each party choosing its own paths. Active-adversary protocol: O(log^2 lambda) rounds and O(log^4 lambda) onions transmitted by every participant per round (lambda = security parameter). Introduces the checkpoint-onion technique and the mixing/equalizing analysis.
bitmessage_link: Gives provable anonymity at polylog overhead, in contrast with O(N) flooding.

title: On the Complexity of Anonymous Communication Through Public Networks
note: This is the source of the 'Dropping-Bound' in the SoK on performance bounds. Upper bound (Thm 3): onion routing that tolerates a polylog (in lambda) number of dropped onions, is anonymous against an active adversary corrupting a constant fraction kappa<1/2 of parties, with polylog rounds and polylog onions per party per round. Lower bound (Thm 4): if an onion routing protocol is weakly robust (delivers to senders whose onions are never dropped) and computationally anonymous against an adversary that corrupts a constant fraction of parties and drops at most f(lambda)=O(log lambda) onions, then its onion cost is omega(f(lambda)) (i.e. super-logarithmic per party). Thm 1: mixing + equalizing imply anonymity; Thm 2: anonymity implies equalizing.
bitmessage_link: Matches the ALU18 upper bound; both far below the O(N) per-message cost of flooding.

title: How to Bootstrap Anonymous Communication
note: Defines anonymous steganography: a leaker embeds a long document in public content and sends a short key over a small anonymous channel. Construction via circuit obfuscation. Lower bound (Thm 2): no reactive anonymous steganography scheme exists with key length s(lambda)=O(log lambda); a PPT adversary identifies the leaker with probability at least q + (1-q)/n - eps unless the key is super-logarithmic. Bootstrapping a large anonymous channel needs a super-logarithmic-size anonymous seed.
bitmessage_link: Bound on how little anonymous channel is needed to carry bulk data; relates to public-bulletin designs that hide the recipient but not the poster.

title: Do Dummies Pay Off? Limits of Dummy Traffic Protection in Anonymous Communications
note: No closed-form impossibility theorem; analytic limit via least-squares: the adversary's profiling error is characterised as a function of user behaviour, mix behaviour and the dummy strategy (least squares disclosure attack, LSDA). For a timed pool mix the analysis yields the optimal dummy strategy for a given privacy target, and shows dummy traffic buys protection against long-term profiling only up to a computable limit.
bitmessage_link: Long-term profiling of persistent senders survives per-round cover traffic; relevant to Bitmessage's pseudo-random dummy ('getpubkey', fake msgs) cost versus intersection resistance.

title: Meet the Family of Statistical Disclosure Attacks
note: Unified framework comparing SDA variants and the least-squares disclosure attack as estimators of senders' behavioural profiles from sets of observed receivers. No bound; comparison of estimator variance.
bitmessage_link: Intersection and profiling attacks defeat the receiver ambiguity that flooding provides once a user is persistent.

title: Understanding the Effects of Real-World Behavior in Statistical Disclosure Attacks
note: Evaluates the least-squares disclosure attack on traffic generated from real datasets rather than synthetic uniform user models; finds the usual models do not fit realistic user behaviour and extends the accuracy analysis.
bitmessage_link: Measured user behaviour (bursty, non-uniform) is what makes recipient-hiding by large anonymity sets weaker in practice.

title: TASP: Towards Anonymity Sets that Persist
note: Problem statement: a global passive adversary shrinks the set of potential recipients over time by intersecting online sets. TASP groups clients into persistent anonymity sets; ~8% bandwidth overhead dramatically lengthens the time to a successful intersection attack.
bitmessage_link: Intersection attacks on the anonymity set; a flooding network gives a fixed large set but users who go offline still leak.

title: A Probabilistic Analysis of Onion Routing in a Black-box Model
note: UC black-box model of onion routing against an adversary that controls a fraction b of routers and knows priors on user destinations. As the network grows, user u's anonymity is worst either when others always choose the destination u is least likely to visit or when they always choose the destination u chooses. Worst-case anonymity against fraction b of routers is comparable to best-case anonymity against fraction sqrt(b).
bitmessage_link: Quantifies how adversary priors on destinations degrade anonymity; relevant to non-uniform recipient popularity.

title: Provably Secure and Practical Onion Routing
note: UC ideal functionality F_OR for onion routing; derives the exact security properties required of onion construction/processing algorithms and key exchange (predictably malleable symmetric encryption, strengthened integrity); proves forward secrecy; realises the black-box model of Feigenbaum-Johnson-Syverson so its anonymity metrics apply to the protocol.
bitmessage_link: Reference UC treatment for relay-based anonymity; Kuhn et al. later find gaps in this proof family.

title: AnoA: A Framework for Analyzing Anonymous Communication Protocols
note: Definition: a protocol P provides (eps, delta)-sender anonymity iff it is (eps, delta)-alpha-IND-CDP for the adjacency function alpha_SA (challenge rows differ only in the sender); likewise sender unlinkability (alpha_UL) and relationship anonymity. (eps,delta)-alpha-IND-CDP: Pr[adversary outputs 0 | b=0] <= e^eps Pr[outputs 0 | b=1] + delta. Unifies anonymity with computational differential privacy.
bitmessage_link: Gives the (eps, delta) vocabulary used by Vuvuzela-style DP accounting and for comparing flooding with mixing.

title: TUC: Time-sensitive and Modular Analysis of Anonymous Communication
note: Universal-composability-style framework (TUC) with a notion of time and sequential activation, enough to model traffic-correlation and website-fingerprinting timing attacks on onion routing; compositional proofs; applied to a Tor website-fingerprinting countermeasure.
bitmessage_link: Timing attacks (the source-timing weakness of immediate flooding) need a time-aware model; TUC is the formal tool.

title: (Nothing else) MATor(s): Monitoring the Anonymity of Tor's Path Selection
note: Rigorous anonymity bounds in an extension of AnoA, applied to Tor's path selection using the public consensus and server descriptors; real-time anonymity monitor on Tor Metrics data; proposes an alternative path selection with stronger guarantees at no performance cost.
bitmessage_link: A measurement-driven way to quote an (eps, delta) for a deployed network, which Bitmessage lacks.

title: A Formal Treatment of Onion Routing
note: First UC ideal functionality for onion routing and the onion-layer security properties (onion-correctness, onion-integrity, onion-security) a scheme must satisfy to realise it; the template that Backes et al. (2012) and Kuhn et al. (2020) revisit. Preliminary-version PDF.
bitmessage_link: Foundational formal definition against which the onion-routing proofs of later systems are measured.

title: A terminology for talking about privacy by data minimization: Anonymity, Unlinkability, Undetectability, Unobservability, Pseudonymity, and Identity Management (v0.34)
note: Canonical vocabulary: anonymity of a subject = not identifiable within an anonymity set of all possible subjects; unlinkability of items of interest = adversary cannot sufficiently distinguish whether they are related; unobservability = items indistinguishable from random noise and sender/recipient anonymous. Defines sender/recipient anonymity, relationship anonymity, undetectability.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage claims recipient anonymity by ambiguity (an anonymity set of all stream nodes); this is the terminology in which that claim is stated.

title: On Privacy Notions in Anonymous Communication
note: Formalises privacy goals (sender/receiver anonymity, unlinkability, relationship anonymity, with message-level variants and 'L-bar' lower-case ones) as indistinguishability notions built from building blocks, and proves a complete hierarchy: for every pair of notions which is strictly stronger. Resolves inconsistencies between AnoA, Hevia-Micciancio, Bohli-Pashalidis and earlier definitions.
bitmessage_link: Fixes which notion 'recipient anonymity by flooding' corresponds to and what it implies.

title: Breaking and (Partially) Fixing Provably Secure Onion Routing
note: Shows the proof strategy of Camenisch-Lysyanskaya / Backes et al. (prove a protocol realises the ideal functionality F_OR, inherit its privacy) is broken: the ideal functionality itself does not provide the properties assumed. Gives a simple link-sender-to-receiver attack on HORNET's data phase, similar attacks on TARANET/Sphinx-family, and a Sphinx padding flaw; proposes improved properties and a partial fix.
bitmessage_link: Warns that 'provably secure by UC realisation' claims for Sphinx-like packet formats need re-checking.

title: Onion Routing with Replies
note: Security definitions and a provably secure construction for onion routing with replies (bidirectional), repairing the flaws exposed in the unidirectional case; gives the privacy notion hierarchy usable for replies.
bitmessage_link: Reply paths matter for two-way recipient privacy (Bitmessage has none; replies are separate flooded objects).

title: Cryptographic Shallots: A Formal Treatment of Repliable Onion Encryption
note: UC ideal functionality for repliable onion encryption (correctness, integrity, security of onions with reply headers) and a construction; underlies the 2022-24 provable onion routing line of Ando-Lysyanskaya-Upfal.
bitmessage_link: Formal basis for reply onions, absent in Bitmessage.

title: Untagging Tor: A Formal Treatment of Onion Encryption
note: Formal security notions for multi-layer onion encryption (the Tor relay-cell setting) including resistance to tagging attacks, shows the deployed Tor design cannot meet them, and proposes a fix based on a tweakable wide-block cipher.
bitmessage_link: Formalises the integrity (anti-tagging) property that Bitmessage's static-key layering never attempts.

title: Bruisable Onions: Anonymous Communication in the Asynchronous Model
note: First provably anonymous onion routing in the asynchronous (no synchronised rounds) model; bruisable onion encryption lets a relay damage a delayed onion so chronic delays make it undeliverable, blocking timing attacks. Removes the synchrony assumption underlying the trilemma and Ando et al.'s round-based bounds.
bitmessage_link: Asynchronous operation is the realistic setting for Bitmessage-like networks; prior provable bounds assume rounds.

title: Vuvuzela: Scalable Private Messaging Resistant to Traffic Analysis
note: DP accounting: Thm 1: adding noise ceil(max(0, Laplace(mu, b))) to the single-access dead-drop count m1 and ceil(max(0, Laplace(mu/2, b/2))) to the double-access count m2 is (eps, delta)-DP for changes of up to 2 in m1 and 1 in m2, with eps = 4/b and delta = exp((2-mu)/b). Parameters b = 4/eps, mu = 2 - 4 ln(delta)/eps. Adaptive composition over k rounds: mu grows only with sqrt(k). Operating point eps = ln 2, delta = 1e-4 for 200,000 rounds (cover story within 2x). Computational DP only.
bitmessage_link: Replaces Bitmessage's flood-everything with bounded noise: privacy loss per round is quantified (eps, delta) rather than trusting set size.

title: Stadium: A Distributed Metadata-Private Messaging System
note: Thm 8.1: a mechanism adding Pois(lambda) noise to an observable X is (eps, delta)-DP for changes of 1 in X with eps = ln(1 + c*sqrt(lambda)/lambda) and delta = e^{-lambda} (e*lambda)^{lambda + c*sqrt(lambda)} / (lambda + c*sqrt(lambda))^{lambda + c*sqrt(lambda)} (c>0 trades eps for delta); composition via Thm 8.4. With chain length 6, 4.6M users at 120 s latency: e^eps = 18.4, 5.3 and 3.5 at 50, 75 and 100 (servers; the paper text says 'users'); extrapolated 500 servers gives e^eps = 1.5, at delta = 1e-4. Shows DP privacy improves with more servers at fixed latency.
bitmessage_link: Scales DP-noise messaging horizontally, the opposite scaling law to flooding (cost grows with users, not nodes).

title: Karaoke: Distributed Private Messaging Immune to Passive Traffic Analysis
note: Introduces optimistic indistinguishability: in the common case (no active attack, no lost messages) the adversary's view is exactly independent of who talks to whom (no leakage under passive analysis), and clients detect when information may leak, so (eps, delta)-DP noise (single/double access noise lambda1, lambda2) is only needed against active attacks. Efficient noise verification via Bloom filters. 6.8 s latency for 2M users, 5-10x better than Vuvuzela and Stadium.
bitmessage_link: Shows DP noise can be avoided against passive observers, a stronger property than Bitmessage's set-size ambiguity.

title: Tight on Budget? Tight Bounds for r-Fold Approximate Differential Privacy
note: Privacy buckets: numerical method computing provable upper and lower bounds on the (eps, delta) of r-fold composition of a mechanism by tracking the privacy-loss distribution. Lower bounds almost meet upper bounds, so no significantly tighter accounting exists for the tested mechanisms; matches the KOV composition theorem for the Laplace mechanism and improves over KOV, concentrated DP and the moments accountant for Gauss, SGD and timing-leakage mechanisms. Motivated by anonymous communication (Vuvuzela-style) noise calibration.
bitmessage_link: Sharper accounting than the Vuvuzela/Stadium composition theorem for the number of rounds a user can safely send.

title: What's a Little Leakage Between Friends?
note: Compromised-friend attack on all metadata-private messaging systems of the time: a malicious friend learns whether a user is sending other messages, enabling intersection/disclosure attacks. Abstracted as the exclusive call-centre problem; no efficient computational-assumption solution found. Private answering machine constructed only under a bounded number of friends, accepting that bound as leakage.
bitmessage_link: Applies to any scheme where a contact can observe a user's activity bit; addresses the 'chan' / known-counterparty weakness in Bitmessage.

title: Formal Security Definition of Metadata-Private Messaging
note: Complete simulation/indistinguishability-style definition of metadata-private messaging (MPM) that accounts for compromised friends, asynchronous per-client rounds and multiple concurrent conversations; shows Addra-style systems proved only at PIR level fall to a variant of the compromised-friend attack; protocol (Anysphere) shown to satisfy the definition.
bitmessage_link: First end-to-end definition of what 'hiding who talks to whom' must mean for a messaging system, not only its transport.

title: The Capacity of Private Information Retrieval
note: Information-theoretic PIR capacity (retrieved bits per downloaded bit) for K messages replicated on N non-colluding databases is C = (1 + 1/N + 1/N^2 + ... + 1/N^{K-1})^{-1}. A single server (N=1) must download everything (C = 1/K).
bitmessage_link: Fixes the download cost of hiding which message is read: Bitmessage 'download everything' is capacity-optimal for one server.

title: Private Information Retrieval with Sublinear Online Time
note: Offline/online PIR with sublinear online server time and no extra server storage. Lower bound (Thm 23): for a computationally secure offline/online PIR scheme where the client downloads C bits offline and the server stores the database in original form and probes T bits online, C * T >= Omega-tilde(n) (n = database bits). Shows the two-server and FHE-based single-server schemes are optimal up to logarithmic factors in this model.
bitmessage_link: Compression of the 'download all' cost used by PIR-based replacements of flooding.

title: Limits of Preprocessing for Single-Server PIR
note: Lower bound for computationally secure single-server PIR with r-bit public hint and expected online time t: t*r = Omega(n log n) when r = Omega(log n); t = Omega(n) when r = O(log n). Holds even with error probability 1/n^2 and distinguishing advantage 1/n. Improves the t*r = Omega(n) bound of Beimel et al. (2004). Cell-probe model via cell sampling.
bitmessage_link: Limits how far PIR preprocessing can cut the cost of reading a message privately.

title: Lower Bounds for PIR with Preprocessing from Blackbox Cryptography
note: Unconditional: if the client stores s bits about an n-bit database, then answering k = Omega(s) queries requires either Omega(n/s) amortized online communication or Omega(n/s) amortized server cryptographic operations, for schemes using any cryptography in a black-box way (random oracles, virtual black-box obfuscation). Tight against known constructions; also bounds for symmetric PIR with client preprocessing.
bitmessage_link: Rules out sublinear-cost private retrieval by black-box means, the 'no free lunch' behind trial-decrypt-everything.

title: Unconditional Security using (Random) Anonymous Bulletin Board
note: Key agreement and string OT in the anonymous bulletin board model (Ishai et al. FOCS 2006): 200% throughput improvement for key agreement with a near-optimality proof, 1-round chosen-message random string OT, and a 1-round lower bound for BEC under stated conditions.
bitmessage_link: What can be built on top of an anonymous bulletin board such as a Bitmessage stream.

title: Cryptography from Anonymity
note: An anonymous channel over insecure channels implements unconditionally secure point-to-point channels and hence honest-majority MPC; anonymity cannot yield unconditional security without honest majority. Also PIR for many users with near-optimal communication and computation, using secret sharing plus anonymous mixing.
bitmessage_link: Shows what an anonymous broadcast board (as a Bitmessage stream tries to be) is worth as a cryptographic resource.

title: On the Inherent Anonymity of Gossiping
note: Source anonymity of gossip measured by eps-DP against f curious nodes. Thm 5 (universal lower bound): for any connected graph G of size n, f>1 curious nodes and any gossip protocol P, if P satisfies eps-DP against an average-case or worst-case adversary then eps >= ln(f-1); moreover if the vertex connectivity kappa(G) <= f, P cannot satisfy eps-DP with finite eps against a worst-case adversary. Thm 8: on (d,lambda)-expander graphs cobra-walk gossip has tangible eps; tight trade-off between dissemination time and source anonymity (rho parameter); technique extends to Dandelion.
bitmessage_link: Direct theory for flood-vs-route: pure flooding from the source reveals the first contacted curious node; no gossip scheme beats eps = ln(f-1).

title: Spy vs. Spy: Rumor Source Obfuscation
note: Adaptive diffusion: spreading protocol that is fast and, against an adversary observing a snapshot of the spread, achieves perfect obfuscation of the source on an infinite regular tree: all infected users are nearly equally likely to be the origin. Contrasts with standard flooding, which rumor-centrality detects. Experiments on a Facebook graph.
bitmessage_link: Flooding leaks the source's neighbourhood to a snapshot adversary; adaptive diffusion is the formal alternative to Bitmessage/Bitcoin-style flood.

title: Hiding the Rumor Source
note: Journal extension of Spy vs. Spy: adaptive diffusion also treated under timestamp-metadata adversaries; on irregular trees characterises the probability of maximum-likelihood detection via a concentration result over Galton-Watson trees; perfect obfuscation on infinite regular trees under the snapshot model.
bitmessage_link: As Spy vs. Spy.

title: Anonymity Properties of the Bitcoin P2P Network
venue: arXiv 1703.08761 (NeurIPS 2017 as Deanonymization in the Bitcoin P2P Network)
note: Proves that both pre-2015 flooding and post-2015 diffusion in Bitcoin's P2P layer offer poor anonymity on regular-tree topologies against a spy-node adversary (first-spy estimator succeeds with constant probability), validated on a 2015 Bitcoin topology snapshot.
bitmessage_link: Direct analysis of flood-based propagation anonymity; same flooding model as Bitmessage's object propagation.

title: Dandelion: Redesigning the Bitcoin Network for Anonymity
note: Dandelion: stem phase (random line forwarding) then fluff phase (diffusion); near-optimal anonymity against a spy adversary in a d-regular network with provable precision/recall bounds, at low latency overhead.
bitmessage_link: Dandelion is the named propagation design for Bitmessage-like source anonymity.

title: Dandelion++: Lightweight Cryptocurrency Networking with Formal Anonymity Guarantees
note: Thm 1: on a random 4-regular graph with graph unknown to the adversary, the maximum expected precision D_OPT <= 8*D_FS + 6p^2 + O(p^3) where D_FS is the first-spy estimator's precision and p the fraction of spies (first-spy is within a constant of optimal; p^2 is a lower bound for any estimator). Thm 2: per-forwarding-scheme precision rates (one-to-one, all-to-one, per-incoming-edge). Thm 3 bounds recall under version checking. Defends against adversaries that disobey the protocol.
bitmessage_link: Formal precision bounds for source privacy of flooding-style broadcast under spy nodes.

title: On the Anonymity of Peer-To-Peer Network Anonymity Schemes Used by Cryptocurrencies
note: Bayesian-inference framework quantifying the anonymity of P2P propagation schemes (diffusion, Dandelion, Dandelion++, Lightning-style and mixnet-based) against colluding nodes; shows the earlier theoretical guarantees weaken under realistic adversary and topology assumptions; gives measures beyond precision/recall.
bitmessage_link: Measured anonymity of the flood-then-stem designs that could harden Bitmessage object origin.

title: On the Impossibility of Efficient Self-Stabilization in Virtual Overlays with Churn
note: In a dynamic restricted-connectivity (darknet/friend-to-friend) network with virtual-overlay greedy routing, either overlay maintenance or routing eventually exceeds polylog(n) cost per operation; self-stabilising virtual overlays cannot be both cheap to maintain and cheap to route in under churn.
bitmessage_link: Rules out cheap routed delivery on a friend-to-friend overlay, the trade-off that motivates flooding in Bitmessage-like designs.

title: A Rudimentary Model for Low-Latency Anonymous Communication Systems
note: Distributed OR model: several lower bounds on the anonymity leakage of deterministic OR algorithms, some showing a trade-off between anonymity and communication complexity; only a trivial, possibly tight bound for randomised OR when communication is ignored; link to open cases in secret sharing.
bitmessage_link: Early abstract model of the anonymity/communication trade-off.

title: Dining Cryptographers are Practical
note: DC-net with optimal collision resolution in which computationally limited disruptors are easy to detect; keeps information-theoretic sender and recipient untraceability of the base protocol.
bitmessage_link: DC-net is the unconditional alternative to flooding for sender anonymity; this paper addresses its collision and disruption problems.

title: Dining Cryptographers with 0.924 Verifiable Collision Resolution
note: Computationally secure DC-net implementing a multiple-access channel with collision resolution achieving maximum stable throughput of 0.924 messages per round (the classic tree-algorithm throughput) and easy disruptor detection.
bitmessage_link: Gives the throughput ceiling of a collision-based DC-net broadcast channel.

title: Arbitrary Length k-Anonymous Dining-Cryptographers Communication
note: Three-phase broadcast (DC-net among a group of size k, then P2P flooding) for blockchain transaction dissemination; extends von Ahn's DC-net protocol to fair delivery of arbitrarily long messages from multiple senders; privacy/security analysis (k-anonymity within the group) and performance evaluation.
bitmessage_link: Combines a small DC-net with flooding to give k-anonymity on a flooded network.

title: Shared-Dining: Broadcasting Secret Shares using Dining-Cryptographers Groups
note: (n,k)-Shamir sharing of the message inside a DC group, then every member floods its share; any k shares reconstruct, fewer reveal nothing. Provides (n - |attackers|)-anonymity for up to k-1 attackers at 10-100 kB/s throughput. Fixes the incentive problem that members of a DC group may refuse to forward.
bitmessage_link: Enforces anonymity in the DC-then-flood design that forwarders have no incentive to honour.

title: Secure Anonymous Broadcast
note: Decentralised anonymous broadcast in which each party sends and computes a polylogarithmic number of bits (and operations) per anonymous bit delivered, in O(log n) rounds; provably secure against traffic analysis with no trusted party, load balanced, tolerating up to n/6 statically scheduled Byzantine parties controlled by a computationally unbounded adversary.
bitmessage_link: Asymptotically beats O(N) flooding for anonymous broadcast, at the price of MPC machinery and an honest supermajority.

title: Towards Provably-Secure Scalable Anonymous Broadcast
note: Anonymous broadcast built from secure multi-party sum (a scalable DC-net generalisation) over small local groups; sketches provable security and scalability, precursor of 'Secure Anonymous Broadcast'.
bitmessage_link: Scalable DC-net style alternative to flooding.

title: Security Analysis of Accountable Anonymity in Dissent
note: Formal definition and proofs for hardened Dissent: provably hides the identity of well-behaved members of a group and provably exposes disruptors (accountability), defining the precise security properties; identifies attacks on the original protocol.
bitmessage_link: Reference formal analysis of a DC-net-with-accountability design.

title: A Survey on Anonymous Communication Systems with a Focus on Dining Cryptographers Networks
note: Survey of anonymous communication systems with emphasis on DC-net variants (Dissent, Verdict, Riposte, PriFi, Herbivore): properties, collision/disruption handling, scalability trade-offs.
bitmessage_link: Positions DC-nets as the strong-anonymity, high-bandwidth end of the design space.

title: A Survey on Routing in Anonymous Communication Protocols
note: Classifies anonymous communication protocols by routing: unstructured vs structured, with path selection, topology and relay-discovery as dimensions; compares security properties (anonymity, censorship resistance) and performance; open problems.
bitmessage_link: Places broadcast/flooding (no routing) at one extreme of the routing taxonomy.

title: SoK: Metadata-Protecting Communication Systems
note: Surveys 31 metadata-protecting communication systems (mixnet, DC-net, PIR and trusted-hardware based) along threat model, goals, latency and bandwidth, and discusses the limits: lower bounds (trilemma-style) and the cost of each design class.
bitmessage_link: Places Bitmessage-like broadcast beside the 31 systems reviewed.

title: SoK: Secure Messaging
note: Systematises secure messaging along trust establishment, conversation security (forward secrecy, future secrecy, deniability, asynchronicity, multi-device) and transport privacy (hiding social graph and metadata); compares dozens of deployed and proposed systems and ranks approaches by usability, security and adoption.
bitmessage_link: Frame of reference for the forward-secrecy and transport-privacy properties Bitmessage lacks.

title: Mixnet Research Review
note: Selected overview of decades of mixnet research with focus on Katzenpost, HOPR, 0KN and Nym; includes 'compromising on latency and compromising on bandwidth', the trilemma view of design choices.
bitmessage_link: Practitioner summary of the latency-vs-bandwidth compromise.

title: Safely Measuring Tor
note: PrivCount: secure aggregation and differentially private noise for Tor measurements; measurement study finds 710,000 users connected but only 550,000 active at a time, Web traffic is 91% of data bytes, and relay policy strictness affects the application mix.
bitmessage_link: Method for measuring the real anonymity-set size and behaviour of a deployed network, which has no analogue for Bitmessage.

title: Understanding Tor Usage with Privacy-Preserving Measurement
note: Privacy-preserving (PrivCount-based) measurement of Tor usage: shares of traffic by application and destination popularity, onion-service use, and sizes of user populations; shows that Tor user behaviour is less uniform than commonly modelled.
bitmessage_link: Empirical anonymity-set and behaviour data that shape any 'k users' ambiguity claim.

title: Users Get Routed: Traffic Correlation on Tor by Realistic Adversaries
note: Quantifies Tor path compromise under realistic user models and adversaries (relays, ASes, IXPs): typical users are far more exposed than earlier uniform-user analyses; e.g. large probabilities of path compromise within months. Model-driven measurement of anonymity.
bitmessage_link: Shows realistic user behaviour, not the static set size, determines achievable anonymity.

title: Trawling for Tor Hidden Services: Detection, Measurement, Deanonymization
note: Harvests hidden-service descriptors via HSDir position manipulation, measures popularity (request counts) and population (e.g. a botnet's size) of hidden services, and shows deanonymisation of service location.
bitmessage_link: Measures a decentralised rendezvous directory the way a Bitmessage stream could be measured.

title: An Empirical Study of the I2P Anonymity Network and its Censorship Resistance
note: Active measurement of I2P (no central directory): estimates network size and churn, characterises peers and geography, and tests blocking; shows censors can enumerate the network with modest resources.
bitmessage_link: I2P is a directory-free decentralised anonymity network whose size must be measured empirically; analogous to enumerating Bitmessage nodes.

title: Measuring Freenet in the Wild: Censorship-resilience under Observation
note: Measurement study plus code analysis of the fully decentralised Freenet: tens of thousands of users with unusually long online times compared to other P2P systems; topology control mechanisms are suboptimal for routing; yields a realistic user model.
bitmessage_link: Observed uptime of users in a decentralised anonymity system (long sessions), relevant to intersection attacks on persistent senders.

title: AnNotify: A Private Notification Service
note: Private notification service from anonymous channels, sharding, dummy queries and Bloom filters: the concrete advantage of an adversary observing multiple queries is calculated; extensions to presence and broadcast notifications and to message-arrival notification for anonymous communication.
bitmessage_link: Hides which mailbox a recipient polls, the receiver-privacy problem Bitmessage solves by downloading everything.

title: Divide and Funnel: A Scaling Technique for Mix-Networks
venue: IACR ePrint 2021/1685 (later published; venue not verified)
note: Scaling technique distributing the public-key work over many nodes without disconnecting paths; sample anonymous broadcast protocol Streams with provable 'one-in-a-billion' unlinkability, 16 s latency at one million messages.
bitmessage_link: A provably unlinkable anonymous broadcast with throughput numbers, comparable to a flood.

title: Are continuous stop-and-go mixnets provably secure?
note: First provable anonymity analysis of continuous-time stop-and-go mixnets (Loopix/Nym style) in a model with real-time delays, in contrast to round-based proofs; quantifies anonymity against a global passive adversary and shows (eps, delta) bounds depending on delay and cover traffic.
bitmessage_link: Extends the trilemma setting from rounds to continuous time, matching real deployments.

title: Improving Signal's Sealed Sender
note: Shows Signal's Sealed Sender conceals the sender only until delivery receipts are observed: a statistical disclosure attack over a small number of messages recovers conversation partners (receipts leak the timing link); proposes mitigations.
bitmessage_link: Demonstrates the SDA weakness against recipient-visible metadata, the same weakness class as Bitmessage's static addresses.

title: Poster: No safety in numbers: traffic analysis of sealed-sender groups in Signal
note: Extends the Martiny et al. statistical disclosure attack from deanonymising pairs to deanonymising entire group conversations in Signal's sealed-sender mechanism.
bitmessage_link: Group traffic analysis; bears on Bitmessage chans whose membership is public to everyone holding the passphrase.

title: Metadata-private Messaging without Coordination
note: Metadata-private messaging where users do not coordinate rounds or online times, relevant to the user-coordination assumption of the comprehensive trilemma.
bitmessage_link: Bears on whether asynchronous users can obtain metadata privacy without Bitmessage-style flooding.

title: Mixnets on a Tightrope: Quantifying the Leakage of Mix Networks Using a Provably Optimal Heuristic Adversary
note: Provably optimal heuristic adversary for mix networks and a method to quantify (eps, delta)-style leakage of a given mixnet configuration; tighter than prior analytical anonymity bounds. Exact statement not read: no legal open copy found (IEEE only).
bitmessage_link: Gives a tighter measure of anonymity per mixnet configuration than the trilemma-type necessary conditions.
